questions.question: What are the core concepts in Spring Batch — Job, Step, Chunk, and Tasklet — and how do they relate to each other?
questions.title: Spring Batch Core Concepts: Job, Step, Chunk, and Tasklet
questions.direct_answer: A Job is the top-level container representing an entire batch process, composed of one or more Steps executed in sequence or conditionally. Each Step can follow either a chunk-oriented model (read-process-write in fixed-size chunks) or a Tasklet model (a single custom unit of work). Together, they give you fine-grained control over large-volume data processing with built-in restart and retry support.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Spring Batch's execution model before writing any code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Tasklet with Chunk — candidates often think Tasklet is just a simpler Step, not realizing they are mutually exclusive execution strategies within a Step
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention JobRepository, JobExecution, and StepExecution as the persistence layer that enables restartability — most candidates skip this

sections.title: Spring Batch's Chunk Model Is Not Just 'Process Records in Groups' — It's a Specific Transaction Boundary Design
sections.content:
Spring Batch was designed for one problem: processing millions of records reliably, with the ability to recover from failures without reprocessing everything. The domain model was designed around that constraint.

A **Job** is the top-level unit of work — 'process today's orders', 'generate monthly invoices'. A Job is composed of **Steps**, each of which does one discrete piece of the work. Each Step chooses one of two mutually exclusive execution strategies.

**Chunk-oriented processing** is the standard model: read N items → process each → write all N in a single transaction. The chunk size is the commit interval — every N items, the transaction commits and progress is persisted. If the job fails at item 7001 with chunk size 100, it restarts at item 7001 (the last committed chunk boundary), not at item 1.

**Tasklet** is for everything that isn't record-by-record processing: downloading a file, sending an email, truncating a staging table, calling an external API once. A Tasklet is a `RepeatStatus.FINISHED` or `RepeatStatus.CONTINUABLE` return from a single `execute()` method. **Chunk and Tasklet are mutually exclusive** — a step is either chunk-oriented or tasklet-based. This is the `common_mistake` the interviewer is checking: candidates who think Tasklet is a simplified chunk step.

Spring Batch persists execution state in a **JobRepository** — backed by a relational database. Every Job, Step, and chunk execution is recorded. This metadata enables restartability, auditing, and multi-instance coordination.

The distinction between Chunk and Tasklet is **the most common mistake** this question tests. Candidates often describe Tasklet as a 'simpler chunk step' — it isn't. They are mutually exclusive execution strategies. You cannot have both a chunk-oriented reader/writer AND a Tasklet on the same Step. Choose one: chunk model for iterating over records, Tasklet model for discrete one-time operations.

sections.title: The Transaction Boundary in Chunk Processing — Why Write Phase Failure Is Different From Read Failure
sections.content:
Understanding the chunk transaction boundary explains most Spring Batch debugging. Each chunk runs inside a single transaction that spans the entire read-process-write cycle for those N items.

The read phase calls `ItemReader.read()` repeatedly until the chunk size is reached or `null` is returned (data exhausted). Read failures are handled per-item and can be configured with retry and skip policies. **But read failures don't affect the transaction** — they happen before the transaction boundary or during item reading within the chunk.

The **write phase is different.** The entire chunk's list of processed items is passed to `ItemWriter.write(Chunk<O> items)` in one call. If the write fails, the entire chunk transaction rolls back — all N items that were successfully read and processed are discarded and must be reprocessed. This is the architectural reason Spring Batch recommends keeping ItemWriter idempotent.

The commit interval is the key tuning parameter. Too small (chunk size 1) means one transaction per item — safe but slow due to commit overhead. Too large (chunk size 10,000) means a failure partway through requires reprocessing thousands of items. For most workloads, 100-500 items per chunk balances throughput with restart granularity.

`@StepScope` is essential for readers and writers that depend on job parameters or runtime data. Without it, a singleton reader shared across multiple job executions would maintain state between runs — a subtle bug that only manifests when running multiple jobs concurrently.

sections.title: The JobRepository and Execution Metadata — What Happens Under the Hood at Startup
sections.content:
When a Job is launched, Spring Batch creates a **JobInstance** — the combination of Job name and JobParameters. If this combination has never run before, it's a new instance. If it has run before and failed, the existing instance restarts from the last checkpoint.

Spring Batch creates tables in your database: `BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE`, `BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION`, `BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_PARAMS`, `BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION`. The schema ships with Spring Batch — `schema-h2.sql`, `schema-mysql.sql`, etc. For tests, an in-memory H2 database with the schema is convenient. **Never use the in-memory `MapJobRepositoryFactoryBean` in production** — it can't persist state across restarts.

The **JobExecution** records the state of a single run attempt: start time, end time, exit status (`COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `STOPPED`). If a Job runs twice with the same parameters and the first run completed successfully, Spring Batch throws a `JobInstanceAlreadyCompleteException` on the second launch — protecting against accidental re-runs. To force a new run for the same business parameters, use `RunIdIncrementer` to add a technical `run.id` parameter.

In production, run only one instance of a given Job with given parameters at a time. Spring Batch doesn't prevent concurrent execution by default — configure your scheduler to prevent overlap or use Spring Batch's `@JobScope` and `JobExecutionDecider` for execution flow control.

The **interview insight** the `to_stand_out` field targets: most candidates describe Spring Batch as 'processes records in batches' and stop there. The JobRepository is the feature that actually differentiates Spring Batch from writing a simple for-loop with a batch insert. Without JobRepository persistence, you get no automatic restart, no audit trail, no idempotency protection, and no visibility into what failed. It's the metadata model that makes Spring Batch suitable for production financial and operational batch processing. Mentioning this demonstrates you've actually used it in production rather than just read about it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Job → Steps → Chunk/Tasklet is the hierarchy** — a `Job` is a complete batch process; a `Step` is one phase (read, process, write or a single task); `Chunk` and `Tasklet` are the two execution models for a step.
- **`JobRepository` persists every execution — it is not optional** — Spring Batch stores `JobInstance`, `JobExecution`, and `StepExecution` in the database; without it, restart, skip, and retry do not work.
- **Chunk processing is transactional per chunk, not per record** — a chunk of 100 items is read, processed, and written inside one transaction; a write failure rolls back only that chunk's 100 items.
- **Tasklet is for single operations that are not read-process-write** — file cleanup, API calls, DDL operations, or sending a completion notification; implement `Tasklet` and return `RepeatStatus.FINISHED`.
- **`JobInstance` = Job + JobParameters; `JobExecution` = one run attempt** — re-running a failed job with the same parameters creates a new `JobExecution` for the existing `JobInstance`, not a new instance.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Batch structures batch processing around a clear hierarchy: Job → Step → Chunk or Tasklet. Every level has a well-defined responsibility and is persisted to the `JobRepository`.

**The hierarchy**
- `Job`: the overall batch process — 'import monthly invoices'; composed of one or more Steps in sequence or conditionally
- `Step`: one phase of the job — 'read from CSV', 'validate records', 'write to database'; each step has its own execution status and can be restarted independently
- `Chunk`: the read-process-write model for a step; reads N items, processes each, writes the batch — all inside one transaction
- `Tasklet`: a single operation for a step — not a read-process-write loop; `execute()` returns `RepeatStatus.FINISHED` or `RepeatStatus.CONTINUABLE`

**`JobRepository` — the persistence layer**
- Stores `JobInstance` (logical job run), `JobExecution` (physical attempt), `StepExecution` (per-step state)
- Enables: restart from the last successful checkpoint; skip counting; retry tracking; execution history
- Spring Boot auto-configures `JobRepository` using the application's `DataSource`

**Chunk transaction model**
- Chunk size 100: reads 100 records, processes each, writes all 100 in one transaction
- A write failure rolls back only that chunk — already committed chunks are not re-processed on restart
- Larger chunks = fewer transactions = better throughput; smaller chunks = finer-grained checkpointing

questions.question: How do ItemReader, ItemProcessor, and ItemWriter work together in Spring Batch chunk processing?
questions.title: ItemReader, ItemProcessor, and ItemWriter: Chunk Processing in Spring Batch
questions.direct_answer: In chunk-oriented processing, ItemReader reads one item at a time until the chunk size is reached, ItemProcessor optionally transforms or filters each item, and ItemWriter receives the complete chunk as a list to persist in a single transaction. This separation of concerns makes each piece independently testable and swappable without touching the others.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can wire a real-world data pipeline and understands the transaction boundary at the write phase
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning null from ItemProcessor to skip an item is correct, but many candidates try to throw an exception instead, which triggers retry/skip logic unintentionally
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that ItemReader.read() returns null to signal end-of-data, and that ItemWriter receives a Chunk<O> (Spring Batch 5) rather than a plain List

sections.title: The Chunk Pipeline Is a Transaction Loop, Not a Stream — Understanding What Happens When Processing Fails Mid-Chunk
sections.content:
ItemReader, ItemProcessor, and ItemWriter are the three roles in Spring Batch's chunk-oriented processing pipeline. What makes the model non-obvious is the **transaction boundary**: read happens outside the commit scope, but the write of all processed items in a chunk happens inside one atomic transaction.

The flow per chunk: call `ItemReader.read()` until the chunk size is reached (or null signals end-of-data) → collect items → pass each through `ItemProcessor.process()` → collect surviving items → call `ItemWriter.write(chunk)` with the entire list in one transaction. The critical insight: **ItemWriter receives a list, not a single item.** This enables batch inserts (`JdbcBatchItemWriter`, `JpaItemWriter`) that are 10-100x faster than individual inserts.

**Returning null from ItemProcessor** is the correct way to filter items. The null-returned item is silently discarded — it will not appear in the ItemWriter's list. Many candidates try to throw an exception to skip items, which triggers retry logic and potentially rolls back the chunk. Null-return is the clean skip signal.

The transaction boundary also explains why **write-phase failures are more expensive than read-phase failures.** If ItemWriter fails partway through a chunk, the entire chunk rolls back — all the read and processing work is repeated on the next restart from the last committed checkpoint. Design ItemWriters to be idempotent to tolerate this re-execution safely.

Spring Batch 5 changed the `ItemWriter` interface signature: `write(List<T> items)` became `write(Chunk<T> chunk)`. The `Chunk` object wraps the list but also carries the `ChunkContext`, making it possible to access step context metadata inside the writer. If you're migrating from Spring Batch 4 to 5, this is the breaking change that requires updating custom `ItemWriter` implementations. The Spring Data and JDBC built-in writers (`JpaItemWriter`, `JdbcBatchItemWriter`) were updated by the framework.

sections.title: Wiring Reader, Processor, and Writer — The @StepScope Annotation That Solves Concurrent Job Execution
sections.content:
A `FlatFileItemReader` reads CSV files; a `JdbcCursorItemReader` streams from a database query; a `JpaPagingItemReader` uses offset-based pagination. The choice depends on data source and volume. **Cursor-based readers hold a database connection open for the entire step** — appropriate for large datasets but requires a transaction manager that supports long-running transactions. **Paging readers** close the connection after each page, making them safer for very large datasets at the cost of potential gaps if data changes during processing.

`@StepScope` is the annotation that makes readers and writers safe for concurrent job execution and for receiving `@Value("#{jobParameters['key']}")` injection. Without `@StepScope`, the reader bean is a singleton — if two job instances run concurrently, they share the same reader state and corrupt each other's processing. With `@StepScope`, Spring creates a new reader instance for each Step execution.

A `CompositeItemProcessor` chains multiple `ItemProcessor` instances in sequence, applying each in order and passing the result to the next. This is cleaner than a single monolithic processor with mixed concerns — a validation processor, an enrichment processor, and a transformation processor can be developed and tested independently, then composed.

For the `ItemWriter`, prefer **batch-aware writers** over looping implementations. `JdbcBatchItemWriter` issues one batch SQL statement for the entire chunk. Writing one item at a time in a loop inside `ItemWriter.write()` defeats the purpose of chunking — you lose the batch insert optimization that makes chunk processing fast.

**Testing chunk processing** requires special consideration. Use `@SpringBatchTest` (added in Spring Batch 4.1) to get a `JobLauncherTestUtils` that simplifies launching jobs in tests. For isolated step testing, `JobLauncherTestUtils.launchStep("stepName")` runs a single step without executing the full job. Mock the reader with a `ListItemReader` that provides a fixed dataset, run the step, and assert on the writer output or the database state. This pattern catches most chunk-processing bugs — null returns from processor, incorrect chunk size, idempotency failures — without requiring a full integration test setup.

sections.title: Fault Tolerance: Retry, Skip, and the Transaction Interaction You Must Understand
sections.content:
Spring Batch's fault tolerance operates at two levels: **retry** (attempt the same item again) and **skip** (discard the item and continue). Both interact with the transaction boundary in ways that catch candidates off guard.

**Retry** works for transient failures — a `DeadlockLoserDataAccessException` from the database, a temporary network error calling an API in ItemProcessor. Configure `faultTolerant().retry(DeadlockLoserDataAccessException.class).retryLimit(3)` on the step. Spring Batch will reprocess the item up to 3 times before giving up. For retry to work, the reader must support re-reading — database readers do, file readers generally do not without `@StepScope` and savestate.

**Skip** handles poison records — items that consistently fail processing or writing and should be excluded from the result. `skip(ValidationException.class).skipLimit(100)` allows up to 100 items to fail with `ValidationException` before the step itself fails. These skipped items are recorded in step execution metadata for audit.

The subtle interaction: **skip on write failures requires a chunk-level rollback followed by single-item retry.** When a write fails, Spring Batch can't know which item in the chunk caused the failure. It rolls back the chunk, then retries each item individually to identify and skip only the failing item. This means every item in a failed chunk is re-read and re-processed — ensure idempotency in your processor and that readers support repositioning.

For non-transactional operations (sending emails, calling external APIs) in a chunk step, be aware that rollback doesn't undo these effects. Handle compensating logic explicitly or move external calls to a separate Tasklet step that runs after the chunk step completes successfully.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`ItemReader.read()` returns `null` to signal end of data** — Spring Batch calls `read()` in a loop until it returns `null`; throwing an exception is for errors, not end-of-input.
- **`ItemProcessor.process()` returns `null` to skip an item** — the null item is filtered out and does not reach the `ItemWriter`; the skip is not counted unless configured.
- **`ItemWriter.write()` receives the entire chunk as a list** — one write call per chunk; bulk INSERT/UPDATE is possible and recommended; writing item-by-item inside `ItemWriter` defeats chunk batching.
- **`CompositeItemProcessor` chains multiple processors** — useful for validation → transformation → enrichment pipelines; each processor receives the output of the previous one.
- **`ItemReader` implementations are not thread-safe by default** — `FlatFileItemReader` and `JdbcCursorItemReader` maintain cursor state; wrap in `SynchronizedItemStreamReader` for multi-threaded steps.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The chunk-oriented step's three components — `ItemReader`, `ItemProcessor`, `ItemWriter` — each have a specific contract. Understanding the contracts prevents subtle bugs like phantom skips or inefficient writes.

**`ItemReader` — read one item at a time**
- Spring Batch calls `read()` repeatedly until it returns `null`
- `null` = end of input; this is the normal termination signal, not an exception
- Built-in readers: `FlatFileItemReader` (CSV/fixed-width), `JdbcCursorItemReader`, `JdbcPagingItemReader`, `JpaPagingItemReader`, `KafkaItemReader`

**`ItemProcessor` — transform or filter one item**
- Receives one item; returns the transformed item or `null` to skip it
- `null` silently removes the item from the chunk — it does not reach `ItemWriter`
- Stateless by design; thread-safe; can be composed with `CompositeItemProcessor` for pipeline steps

**`ItemWriter` — write the entire chunk**
- Receives `List<T>` — all processed items from the chunk
- Bulk INSERT/UPDATE the entire list in one database call; never loop and write one at a time inside `ItemWriter`
- Built-in writers: `JdbcBatchItemWriter` (batch SQL), `JpaItemWriter`, `FlatFileItemWriter`, `KafkaItemWriter`

**Thread safety**
- `FlatFileItemReader` maintains a file cursor — calling `read()` from multiple threads corrupts the cursor
- Wrap with `SynchronizedItemStreamReader` or use `JdbcPagingItemReader` (which is re-entrant by page) for multi-threaded steps

questions.question: How do Job parameters work in Spring Batch, and how do you restart a failed job from where it left off?
questions.title: Spring Batch Job Parameters and Restarting Failed Jobs
questions.direct_answer: Job parameters uniquely identify a JobInstance — the same Job name plus the same parameters always map to the same instance, preventing duplicate runs. When a job fails, its JobExecution is marked FAILED in the JobRepository, and re-launching with the same parameters triggers a restart that skips already-committed steps and resumes from the last failed or incomplete step.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JobInstance vs JobExecution and the idempotency model Spring Batch enforces
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding a timestamp or run-id parameter every time to force a new JobInstance — valid, but candidates should know it also means losing automatic restart capability for that specific run
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @StepScope and @JobScope for late binding of parameters into readers/writers, and how JobParametersIncrementer enables scheduled reruns

sections.title: Spring Batch's JobInstance Model Enforces Idempotency — And Most Teams Fight It Until They Understand Why It Exists
sections.content:
Spring Batch distinguishes between three concepts that most developers initially conflate: **JobInstance** (what you're processing), **JobExecution** (a specific attempt to process it), and **JobParameters** (the identity of the instance).

A `JobInstance` is identified by the combination of **Job name + JobParameters**. If you run the `orderProcessingJob` with `processingDate=2024-01-15`, Spring Batch creates one JobInstance for that combination. If that run fails and you relaunch with the same parameters, Spring Batch creates a new `JobExecution` for the **same JobInstance** — and restarts from the last committed checkpoint, not from scratch.

If the first run completed successfully (`COMPLETED` status), relaunching with the same parameters throws `JobInstanceAlreadyCompleteException`. This is **intentional** — it prevents accidental re-processing of already-completed business data. If you genuinely need to rerun a completed job (data correction, reprocessing), you have two options: launch with different parameters that reflect the new execution (e.g., a `reprocessing=true` flag), or clean up the execution metadata from the `BATCH_*` tables.

This model is the `common_mistake` target: teams add a timestamp or UUID to parameters on every launch to force uniqueness, avoiding the idempotency constraint. That works but defeats the restart model — each launch is a new instance with no restart capability. The right design separates identity parameters (business keys) from run-control parameters (technical incrementers).

Understanding the difference between `JobInstance` and `JobExecution` is the foundation of the entire restart model. Think of `JobInstance` as the business task ('process March statements for account group A') and `JobExecution` as an attempt to complete that task. One business task may have multiple execution attempts if early attempts fail. Spring Batch records every attempt, and the metadata in `BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION` and `BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION` tells you the exact state of each attempt — what was read, what was committed, where the failure occurred.

sections.title: How Spring Batch Determines Restart Position — The Checkpoint Mechanism
sections.content:
When a failed JobExecution is restarted, Spring Batch uses the **step execution metadata** to determine where to resume. Each Step execution records its status (`COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `STOPPED`), and for chunk steps, the `readCount` (number of items read in the last successful execution) is the checkpoint.

For **paging readers**, the restart position is derived from `readCount` — Spring Batch skips forward by that many items on restart. If 7000 items were processed before failure, the paging reader starts at offset 7000. This requires that the data set is stable between runs — if items were inserted into the query result set between the failed run and the restart, the offset no longer maps to the same item.

For **cursor readers**, restarting requires the cursor to be re-opened from the beginning and skipped forward to `readCount`. Some cursor-based readers support `saveState(false)` to disable restart capability (and process from scratch on restart) — appropriate for short, fast steps where restart overhead exceeds restart benefit.

For **partitioned jobs** (multiple concurrent step instances), each partition maintains its own step execution and checkpoint. A failed partition restarts only its own partition — other completed partitions are not re-executed. This is the scalability advantage of partitioning: partial failure only re-runs the affected partition, not the entire dataset.

sections.title: Designing Job Parameters for Production — Identity, Incrementers, and Operational Flexibility
sections.content:
JobParameters must serve two purposes simultaneously: **identifying the business scope** of a run (what data is being processed) and **enabling operational flexibility** (re-running, forcing new instances, testing). Conflating these two purposes in a single parameter set leads to operational friction.

A clean production parameter design: **business parameters** are the identity — `processingDate`, `region`, `batchType`. These uniquely identify what data the job is processing. **Technical parameters** are additive — `runId` (from `RunIdIncrementer`) creates uniqueness when you need multiple runs against the same business data, such as manual reruns after data corrections.

Job parameters are typed: String, Long, Double, Date. Use the right type — don't pass a date as a String and parse it in the processor. `@Value("#{jobParameters['processingDate']}")` with type `LocalDate` requires a custom converter; using Spring Batch's native Date type and converting is simpler.

**`@JobScope`** is the correct scope for beans that depend on job parameters but not step parameters — configuration beans that read job parameters at job launch time, before any steps execute. Use `@StepScope` for readers and writers that need per-step parameters. Both scopes create beans lazily at the appropriate lifecycle point, not at application startup.

For **scheduled execution**, configure your scheduler (Quartz, Spring `@Scheduled`, Kubernetes CronJob) to pass meaningful parameters — the processing date, not a run timestamp. This makes the `BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_PARAMS` table readable as an audit log of what was processed when, rather than a list of meaningless UUIDs.

**Cleaning up execution metadata** is an operational concern often ignored until the `BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION` table grows to millions of rows and queries slow down. Spring Batch 5 includes a `BatchDataSourceScriptDatabaseInitializer` and a `JobExplorerFactoryBean`, and you can pair a scheduled cleanup job (using Spring Batch itself) that deletes old execution metadata beyond a retention window. Alternatively, set up database partitioning on execution start time. For most organizations, 90 days of execution history is enough for auditing — beyond that, archive to cold storage or delete.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`JobParameters` determine `JobInstance` identity** — same Job name + same parameters = same `JobInstance`; a `JobInstance` can have multiple `JobExecution`s (initial run + restarts).
- **Adding a timestamp parameter forces a new `JobInstance`** — useful for jobs that must re-run from scratch every time; but defeats the restart mechanism for jobs that should resume.
- **A `FAILED` `JobExecution` can be restarted; a `COMPLETED` one cannot by default** — Spring Batch prevents re-running a successfully completed `JobInstance` with the same parameters; use `allowStartIfComplete(true)` per step for idempotent steps.
- **`@StepScope` and `@JobScope` enable late binding of parameters** — `@Value("#{jobParameters['file']}")` in a `@StepScope` bean is evaluated when the step starts, not when the `ApplicationContext` loads.
- **Step restartability depends on `ItemReader` stateful checkpointing** — `FlatFileItemReader` saves its position in `ExecutionContext`; on restart, it seeks to the last committed position and resumes from there.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Batch's restart capability is one of its most powerful features — a job that fails at record 50,000 can resume from record 50,001 rather than starting over. This requires understanding how parameters, instances, and executions relate.

**The identity model**
- `JobInstance` = Job name + `JobParameters`; represents a logical run (e.g., 'import for 2024-01')
- `JobExecution` = one physical attempt of a `JobInstance`; a failed `JobInstance` gets a new `JobExecution` on restart
- `StepExecution` = one attempt of one step within a `JobExecution`; stores `readCount`, `writeCount`, `commitCount`, and the `ExecutionContext` for restart state

**Starting vs restarting**
- First run: `jobLauncher.run(job, params)` creates a new `JobInstance` and a new `JobExecution`
- Restart: `jobLauncher.run(job, sameParams)` finds the existing `FAILED` `JobInstance` and creates a new `JobExecution` for it; steps that completed successfully are skipped
- A `COMPLETED` `JobInstance` cannot be re-launched by default — add `allowStartIfComplete(true)` to steps that need to run again

**Late binding with `@StepScope`**
- `@StepScope @Bean FlatFileItemReader reader(@Value("#{jobParameters['inputFile']}") String file)` — the `file` value is not available at context load time; `@StepScope` defers bean creation until the step starts
- Essential for parameterized readers and writers

questions.question: How do you configure retry and skip logic in Spring Batch to handle transient errors and bad records?
questions.title: Spring Batch Retry and Skip Logic for Fault-Tolerant Batch Jobs
questions.direct_answer: Spring Batch provides built-in retry and skip policies on chunk steps: retry re-attempts processing or writing for a configured exception type up to a limit before failing, while skip silently discards items that cause specified exceptions up to a tolerance count, logging them via a SkipListener. Together they let you build fault-tolerant pipelines that handle transient infrastructure errors and dirty data without stopping an entire batch run.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of where retry and skip apply (read, process, write phases) and the interaction with transactions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Applying skip to write-phase exceptions without considering that a failed write rolls back the entire chunk — Spring Batch uses a binary search strategy to identify the bad item, which surprises many candidates
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the chunk retry rollback cycle and how Spring Batch uses single-item recovery after a write failure to isolate the offending record

sections.title: Skip Logic Handles Bad Records by Discarding Them — Retry Logic Handles Transient Failures by Repeating Them
sections.content:
Batch jobs processing millions of records will encounter failures. The question is: **should the job stop, retry, or skip the bad record?** Spring Batch provides configurable retry and skip policies that handle both transient failures (database timeout, network blip) and permanent failures (malformed data, validation errors) without stopping the entire job.

**Skip logic** tells Spring Batch to ignore certain exceptions and continue processing. `.faultTolerant().skip(ValidationException.class).skipLimit(100)` allows up to 100 validation errors before the job fails. Skipped items are tracked in the JobRepository — you know exactly how many and which items were skipped.

**Retry logic** tells Spring Batch to re-attempt a failed operation. `.retry(DeadlockLoserDataAccessException.class).retryLimit(3)` retries database deadlocks up to 3 times. Retries apply to the **processor and writer** — not the reader. On retry, the chunk is re-processed from scratch (all items re-read from the reader's saved position and re-processed). This is why processor and writer must be idempotent.

sections.title: Combining Retry, Skip, and the Chunk Rollback-Retry Mechanism
sections.content:
When a writer fails (e.g., constraint violation in a batch insert), Spring Batch **rolls back the entire chunk transaction** and enters a retry-then-skip mode. It re-reads the chunk items one by one, processing and writing each individually to identify the specific failing item. The good items succeed; the bad item is skipped (if configured) or the step fails.

This **single-item fallback** is critical for isolating failures in batch writes. A batch INSERT of 100 items fails because of one bad record. Without fallback, all 100 items are lost. With fallback, 99 items are committed and 1 is skipped.

**Skip listeners** (`SkipListener`) capture skipped items for logging, alerting, or writing to an error file. Implement `onSkipInRead()`, `onSkipInProcess()`, and `onSkipInWrite()` to handle skips at each stage.

**Retry + Skip together** means: try the chunk, retry on transient errors (deadlock), and if the error is permanent (validation), skip the individual item. The ordering matters — retry is attempted first; if all retries are exhausted and the exception is skippable, the item is skipped. If it's not skippable, the step fails.

sections.title: Configuring noRollback and Non-Transactional Processors — When You Don't Want Rollback to Undo Side Effects
sections.content:
Not every exception should trigger a chunk rollback. `noRollback(ValidationException.class)` tells Spring Batch that a `ValidationException` is expected and doesn't indicate data corruption — the chunk can continue without rolling back. This is appropriate for exceptions that represent bad input data rather than system failures.

For **non-transactional operations inside a chunk** (sending notifications, calling external APIs), the standard chunk model is problematic: if the write fails after the external call succeeds, the chunk rolls back but the external API call is already done. Use `processor(itemProcessor()).processorTransactional(false)` to mark the processor as non-transactional — its side effects won't be undone on rollback, but the processor must be designed to be safe for re-execution.

Alternatively, restructure the job: a **first step** handles the pure data transformation and database writes (fully transactional), and a **second step** reads the successfully-processed records and sends notifications (side effects). The second step can use a simple Tasklet that reads from the output of step 1, decoupling the transactional core from the non-transactional periphery.

For the **skipListener**, implement `SkipListener<T, S>` to record which items were skipped and why. `onSkipInRead()`, `onSkipInProcess()`, and `onSkipInWrite()` give you the item and the exception, enabling an audit trail of skipped records without stopping the job.

sections.title: Retry with Backoff — Handling Database Deadlocks and Transient Network Failures Without Overwhelming the System
sections.content:
Retry without backoff can make transient failures worse. If 100 concurrent chunk writers all retry immediately after a deadlock, they retry into the same contention — the retry storm can deadlock the database repeatedly. **Exponential backoff** spaces retries out: first retry after 1 second, second after 2 seconds, third after 4 seconds.

Configure backoff on the step: `faultTolerant().retry(DeadlockLoserDataAccessException.class).retryLimit(3).backOffPolicy(exponentialBackoff)` where `exponentialBackoff` is a `ExponentialBackOffPolicy` with initial interval, multiplier, and max interval.

For **retrying at the job level** (not just the step), Spring Batch doesn't have built-in job-level retry. The pattern is to schedule the job with retry logic in the scheduler: if the launch returns `FAILED` exit code, re-launch after a delay. This handles catastrophic failures (database unavailable, disk full) that no step-level retry can fix.

The `RetryListener` interface provides hooks for `onRetry()` and `onError()` — log which exception triggered retry, how many attempts have been made, and how long until the next attempt. This observability is essential for operations: without it, you can't distinguish a healthy job retrying a transient error from a job stuck in an infinite retry loop on a permanent error.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Skip and retry are configured per exception type** — `faultTolerant().skip(ValidationException.class).skipLimit(100)` skips up to 100 validation failures; other exception types still fail the step.
- **Retry on write triggers single-item recovery for that chunk** — when a write fails for a chunk of 10, Spring Batch switches to single-item mode: re-reads and re-writes each item individually to identify the failing one; the good items are re-committed.
- **`SkipListener` is notified for every skipped item** — implement `onSkipInRead`, `onSkipInProcess`, `onSkipInWrite` to log skipped items, write them to a dead-letter file, or alert.
- **`RetryListener` is notified on retry events** — `onError` fires on each retry attempt; `onClose` fires when retries are exhausted; useful for metrics and alerting.
- **Skip in write is the most complex case** — the item has been read and processed; the writer rejects it; Spring Batch re-processes the chunk without the bad item; the processor may have side effects that already occurred.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Batch's fault tolerance features — skip and retry — let batch jobs process millions of records while handling individual failures gracefully instead of aborting the entire job.

**Skip**
- Configure per exception type: `faultTolerant().skip(ParseException.class).skipLimit(1000)`
- A skipped item is counted against `skipLimit`; exceeding the limit fails the step
- `SkipListener` receives every skipped item — use it to write rejected items to a dead-letter file or database table for human review

**Retry**
- `faultTolerant().retry(TransientDataAccessException.class).retryLimit(3)` — retries up to 3 times on transient database errors before failing the chunk
- Use for transient failures (network blip, database deadlock) that are likely to succeed on retry

**The write-failure recovery cycle**
- Chunk of 100 items writes; one item causes a `ConstraintViolationException`; the entire chunk rolls back
- Spring Batch switches to single-item mode: re-reads item 1, re-processes, writes — success; repeats for each item
- The failing item is skipped (if skip is configured) or causes the step to fail
- This is why skip is expensive: each write failure can cause N re-reads and re-processes for the chunk

**Don't skip on write when the processor has side effects**
- If `ItemProcessor` sends an email or calls an API, skipping the write after the processor ran means the side effect already happened
- Design processors to be idempotent or move side effects to the writer

questions.question: What are the key differences between Spring Batch and Spring Integration, and how do they complement each other?
questions.title: Spring Batch vs Spring Integration: When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: Spring Batch is designed for scheduled, finite, high-volume data processing jobs with start/end semantics, restart capability, and transactional chunk processing. Spring Integration is designed for event-driven, continuous, message-based integration workflows connecting heterogeneous systems. They are complementary — Spring Integration can trigger and orchestrate Spring Batch jobs, and Spring Batch can use Spring Integration channels as item sources or sinks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Architectural understanding of when batch processing is appropriate versus event-driven integration, and awareness that both frameworks coexist in the Spring ecosystem
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Spring Integration can replace Spring Batch for bulk data processing — it lacks chunk transactions, job restart, skip/retry policies, and the execution metadata model
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the canonical integration pattern: Spring Integration polls a directory or message queue, and upon detecting new files, launches a Spring Batch job via a JobLaunchingGateway

sections.title: Spring Batch Processes Large Datasets in Scheduled Jobs — Spring Integration Routes Messages in Real-Time Flows
sections.content:
Developers confuse these because both handle data movement. The distinction is **timing and pattern.** Spring Batch is for **scheduled, finite workloads** — process all orders from yesterday, generate a monthly report, migrate data between systems. It starts, processes a known dataset, and completes. Spring Integration is for **continuous, event-driven flows** — route incoming messages, transform data as it arrives, integrate with external systems in real-time.

Spring Batch is **chunk-oriented with transactional checkpointing.** It reads, processes, and writes data in batches with restart capability. Spring Integration is **message-oriented with routing patterns** — channels, filters, transformers, routers, and adapters compose enterprise integration patterns (EIP).

They complement each other. A common pattern: **Spring Integration triggers a Spring Batch job** when a file arrives on an FTP server. Integration detects the file (event), launches the Batch job (processing), and sends a notification when complete (routing). Integration handles the event-driven plumbing; Batch handles the heavy data processing.

sections.title: Batch vs Integration — When, How, and What They Process
sections.content:
The right tool depends on the workload pattern.

| Aspect | Spring Batch | Spring Integration |
|---|---|---|
| **Pattern** | Scheduled, finite dataset | Continuous, event-driven |
| **Processing** | Chunk-oriented (read-process-write) | Message-oriented (route-transform-filter) |
| **Restart** | Yes — resume from last checkpoint | No — messages are processed once or retried |
| **Scaling** | Partitioning, multi-threaded steps | Channel concurrency, thread pools |
| **State** | JobRepository tracks execution | Stateless (or message store for aggregation) |
| **Trigger** | Scheduler, API, file arrival | Continuous — listens for events |
| **Example** | Process 10M bank transactions | Route incoming payments to processors |

**Together they cover the full spectrum:** Integration for real-time event routing and triggering, Batch for heavy scheduled processing. Using Batch for real-time processing is wrong (it's designed for finite datasets). Using Integration for processing 10 million database records is wrong (no checkpointing or restart).

sections.title: When to Use Spring Batch, When to Use Spring Integration, and When to Use Both Together
sections.content:
**Use Spring Batch when:** you have a finite, known dataset to process — yesterday's orders, last month's invoices, records imported from a file or database table. You need restart capability (process 10 million records, fail at 7 million, restart at 7 million). You need chunk-level transaction control, skip/retry policies for bad records, and execution metadata for auditing. Scheduled, 'fire and complete' workloads are the core use case.

**Use Spring Integration when:** you have continuous streams of incoming messages — webhook events, file drops, database polling, or inter-system message routing. You need transformation pipelines (filter, enrich, split, aggregate) that operate on individual messages as they arrive. Spring Integration excels at connecting disparate systems with adapters — SFTP, JMS, Kafka, HTTP endpoints — without custom infrastructure code.

**Use both together for hybrid workloads.** A Spring Integration flow monitors an SFTP server for new files, moves each file to a staging location, and triggers a Spring Batch job to process the file's contents. Spring Integration handles the event-driven trigger (file arrival); Spring Batch handles the reliable bulk processing (chunk commits, restart, skip). This combination is common in ETL pipelines and financial processing systems.

The test: if you can describe the workload as 'process all records in this dataset', use Batch. If you describe it as 'whenever a message arrives, do X', use Integration. If both descriptions apply to different parts of the same system, use both.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring Batch: bulk data processing; Spring Integration: event-driven message routing** — Spring Batch processes large datasets in structured jobs with checkpointing; Spring Integration routes messages between systems in real time.
- **Spring Batch provides restartability, skip, retry, and partitioning** — built for multi-hour batch jobs that may fail and must resume; Spring Integration has no concept of job state or checkpointing.
- **Spring Integration triggers Spring Batch jobs** — canonical pattern: Spring Integration polls an S3 bucket for new files; on detection, it launches a Spring Batch job to process the file; the two frameworks are complementary, not competing.
- **Spring Integration is channel-based; Spring Batch is step-based** — Integration wires message channels, transformers, and routers; Batch defines ordered steps with readers, processors, and writers.
- **Spring Cloud Data Flow orchestrates both** — provides a UI and REST API to define, deploy, and monitor batch jobs and streaming pipelines built with Batch and Integration.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Batch and Spring Integration are often confused because both deal with data pipelines. They solve fundamentally different problems and are frequently used together.

**Spring Batch — structured bulk processing**
- Designed for: processing millions of records from a file or database on a schedule
- Key features: `JobRepository` for state persistence, restart from failure, skip/retry policies, partitioned parallel processing, chunk-level transaction management
- Use when: you have a defined start, a defined end, and need to track how many records were processed, skipped, and committed

**Spring Integration — event-driven message routing**
- Designed for: connecting systems and routing messages in real time
- Key features: message channels, adapters (file system, JMS, AMQP, SFTP, email), transformers, routers, filters
- No concept of job state, checkpointing, or restart — it is a continuous pipeline

**The canonical integration pattern**
- Spring Integration watches an S3 bucket or SFTP folder for new files (inbound file adapter)
- When a file arrives, Integration launches a Spring Batch job with the file path as a `JobParameter`
- Spring Batch reads, processes, and writes the file's records with full fault tolerance

**Decision**
- Bounded dataset, needs restart/skip/retry → Spring Batch
- Continuous event stream, system integration, message routing → Spring Integration
- Both, with Batch triggered by Integration events → standard enterprise pattern
